text:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued certification for the Boeing 737 MAX-10, a completed action that clears a major regulatory hurdle for the aircraft’s commercial entry and stabilizes production timelines for the manufacturer. This decision follows the agency’s adoption of a new airworthiness directive for certain Boeing airplanes, signaling a dual focus on resolving legacy safety mandates while advancing new fleet capabilities [FAA issued certification for the Boeing 737 MAX-10](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/federal-aviation-administration-issues-certification-boeing-737-max-10). Simultaneously, the Transportation Secretary announced the first-ever Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate for electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, a move that establishes a new regulatory pathway for the advanced air mobility sector [Transportation Secretary announced the first-ever Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate for eVTOL aircraft](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/trumps-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-announces-first-ever-special-airworthiness).

Regulatory scrutiny of autonomous vehicle operations intensified as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a probe into Tesla robotaxis for speeding and ignoring school zones. This investigation coincides with reports that NHTSA audited 1,000 Cybercabs, with Tesla targeting a 2026 sale despite the agency’s review [NHTSA opened a probe for Tesla robotaxis speeding and ignoring school zones](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMic0FVX3lxTE8zQThsSmRPZXVoOHRjRmt6QllXU1lQYkJuQ0o1ckdVX2lDbmg0Nk4yTnlyamxqU0lnanc2Qk1sdVJZMlFRUE1BN1lwSFZiVzl3U2NBWFBWN1I5VDA4cEZFUHBEdkNYb1JhLS0xbmtCNlduQ1E?oc=5). The agency’s active enforcement posture contrasts with its proposal to conduct a new Older Novice Driver Study, indicating a broader expansion of data collection efforts regarding driver behavior and safety [NHTSA proposed to conduct a new information collection, Older Novice Driver Study](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/19/2026-21264/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-for).

In the drone sector, the Federal Aviation Administration imposed restrictions on unauthorized drones along the U.S.-Mexico border to counter cartel threats. Multiple reports confirm the agency locked down border airspace to drones through 2027, citing security concerns [FAA imposed a drone ban along the US-Mexico border amid cartel threats](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYkFVX3lxTE0yT2J0U1AwMVB3Z3JUcDN3WmE0ZXBCQmFaNHMwNlpSVExrQjg4MmsteTg1dC10c0xKXzh1a1RXdE5TRlkwcEhNZ2FZRGR6Q2JIWS1hOW01N0QzaFBDWmpUV1h3?oc=5). This action highlights a growing trend of agencies expanding their regulatory reach into drone operations, as evidenced by discussions regarding the Transportation Security Administration’s move into drone regulation [TSA’s move into drone regulation](https://news.google.?oc=5).

The Federal Aviation Administration also proposed a $351,000 civil penalty against Creamer Pilot Services for alleged unauthorized passenger-carrying operations, demonstrating continued enforcement of aviation safety standards [FAA proposed a $351,000 fine against Creamer Pilot Services](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-proposes-351000-fine-against-creamer-pilot-services-alleged-unauthorized-passenger). Additionally, the agency and the National Air Traffic Controllers Association reached a deal to provide air traffic controllers with a 2.8% pay increase, addressing workforce stability within the aviation system [FAA and National Air Traffic Controllers Association reached a deal to provide air traffic controllers with a pay increase](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/trumps-transportation-department-air-traffic-controller-union-announce-28-pay-increase).
